name: Body wraps

card.summary: Spa wraps and sauna suits marketed for slimming; the temporary inch loss is water, per the FDA.
card.aka: Mud wraps, plastic wraps, sauna suits, neoprene wraps
card.note: FDA warns that rapid fluid loss can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

quick.overview:
Body wraps are spa or home treatments in which the torso or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic or neoprene, sometimes after mud or lotion is applied, to produce sweating. Proponents say they slim and tone the body, firm skin and remove toxins.

No clinical studies supporting those claims are cited in reference sources. The US Food and Drug Administration has said that any weight lost is fluid that is quickly replaced.
quick.mechanism: Wrapping and heat cause sweating and temporary water loss and may compress tissue, which can reduce measurements for a short time. The FDA states wraps do not dissolve fat.
quick.risks: The FDA warns that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte disruption. Heat and restriction from tight wraps are additional considerations.

lead: Body wraps are cosmetic or spa treatments in which part of the body is wrapped in bandages, plastic film or neoprene, often after application of mud, herbal preparations or lotions, and sometimes combined with a PVC sauna suit. Wikipedia's article on mud wraps notes that body wraps redirect to it.[1]

Proponents claim the treatment can slim and tone the body, hydrate or firm skin, relax muscles and flush toxins through sweat.[1] The article cites no clinical studies supporting those claims.[1] The US FDA has stated that wraps cause temporary water loss rather than fat loss, that the fluid is quickly replaced, and that rapid excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.[1]
infobox: Bandages, mud, plastic film, neoprene, PVC sauna suits
FDA warning on wraps for weight reduction

paras: In a typical spa treatment, mud or another preparation is applied to the skin and the area is covered with bandages, sometimes inside a plastic or PVC suit, to induce sweating.[1] Consumer versions include neoprene waist trainers and sauna suits worn during exercise.

Wikipedia describes proponents as saying wraps slim, tone, hydrate and firm the body and help with sore muscles and inflammation, and as alleging that they flush out toxins.[1] The article cites no clinical studies for these claims.[1]

The FDA position summarized there is that any weight loss is from fluid and is rapidly regained, that wraps do not dissolve fat even temporarily, and that fat is reduced only when calorie intake is below energy expenditure.[1]

The FDA warning cited in the article states that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.[1] The article's sources date to a 1982 FDA Consumer piece and a 2009 ABC News report.[1]
No studies found. Medical literature on wraps concerns unrelated uses such as burn dressings and neonatal warming, which are not studies of cosmetic slimming wraps.

timeline.event: An FDA Consumer article by Judith Willis warns against body wraps as a weight-reduction method.[1]
ABC News reports on risks of body wraps.[1]

lore.intro: Wraps are mentioned in appearance communities mostly for short-term inch loss before events.

claims.believers: Users and spas report a slimmer measurement after a session.
claims.experts: The FDA states the loss is fluid that is quickly replaced.[1]

claims.believers: Spa marketing says sweating flushes toxins.[1]
claims.experts: No clinical studies supporting detoxification are cited in the reference article.[1]

claims.believers: Proponents describe them as a relaxing, low-risk treatment.
claims.experts: The FDA warns rapid fluid loss can cause dehydration and electrolyte disruption.[1]
